wiki_fulltext:
Hibiscus is a genus of plants in the family Malvaceae native to the tropics and subtropics. The genus is quite large, comprising 319 species. Hibiscus are renowned for their large, showy flowers and those species are commonly known simply as "hibiscus", or less widely known as rose mallow. The genus includes both annual and perennial herbaceous plants, as well as woody shrubs and small trees.
Several species are widely cultivated as ornamental plants, notably Hibiscus syriacus and Hibiscus × rosa-sinensis.


Description


Vegetative characteristics
Hibiscus are annual or perennial, 0.1–4 m tall shrubs, subshrubs, trees, or herbs with alternate, usually stipulate, petiolate leaves with an entire or lobed margin. The leaf venation is pinnate or palmate.


Generative characteristics
The flowers are large and conspicuous. They are trumpet-shaped, with five or more petals, colour from white to pink, red, blue, orange, peach, and from 4–18 cm broad.
Flower colour in certain species, such as H. mutabilis and H. tiliaceus, changes with age. The fruit is a dry five-lobed capsule, containing several seeds in each lobe, which are released when the capsule dehisces (splits open) at maturity. It is of red and white colours. It is an example of complete flowering.


Traits
Known for its hardiness, Hibiscus rosa-sinensis withstands ailments and pests, and is tough in the face of both too much water and/or drought. 


Taxonomy
It was described by Carl Linnaeus in 1753 with Hibiscus syriacus L. as the type species.


Etymology
The generic name is derived from the Greek name ἱβίσκος (hibískos) which Greek botanist Pedanius Dioscorides gave to a plant now scientifically labelled as Althaea officinalis.


Distribution
Hibiscus species are numerous, and are native to a wide variety of tropical and warm temperate regions, from China to East Africa to Hawaii. In Hawaii, there is a question as to whether it was  brought to the island by Polynesian settlers or is indigenous. There are 35 species which are native to the US. Scarlet rosemallow, a Hibiscus species native to Florida, thrives in wetlands, as does the less common swamp rosemallow. Rose of Sharon is not a rose, but rather a hibiscus shrub, native to both Northern Israel and Syria. 
There is a great deal of hybridization via grafting of differing Hibiscus species, resulting in cultivars possessing various colors and appearance. Hot houses and indoor spaces enable the flower to thrive outside of tropical and sub-tropical areas. Often these hybrids look very different from. native species of hibiscus.


Botanical Gardens
Hibiscus is a popular plant worldwide in many botanical gardens. The planting and presenting hibiscus dates back to the 1700s at Boboli Gardens, Florence, Italy, and continues to this day.
In Fiji, a project was started to save the country's rare Hibiscus storckii from extinction, via cultivating it in the country's Savurua Botanic Garden on Viti Levu.
Many botanic gardens in the USA showcase hibiscus. The Chicago Botanic Garden contains a wide assortment of hibiscus cultivars in colors ranging from red to peach to purple. The  Brooklyn Botanic Garden appreciates the heartiness and longevity of the flower, as well as its multicolored options, and along with other flowers, highlights hibiscus by its water garden.  There are six endemic hibiscus species in Hawaii, which come in a variety of colors. The Limahuli Botanical Garden (Pacific Tropical Botanical Garden) is rich in a variety of species, including hibiscus. A small sampling of other American gardens which display hibiscus includes the UT Gardens (Tennessee,) the Frelinghuysen Arboretum in New Jersey, and Atlanta Botanical Garden.
Hibiscus is also well presented across Europe. Some examples of locations include Kew Gardens in London, where the rare Clay's Hibiscus is housed, preserved, and propagated. This hibiscus species is severely endangered in its native Hawaii, due to climate change, crowding out by non-native plants, and consumption by wild goats and pigs. Another site is Jardin Extraordinaire in Nantes, France, whose microclimate (several degrees warmer than the general area) allows for the growth of many tropical plants, including hibiscus. Le Gallerie Deglie Uffizi in Italy contains Hibiscus rosa-synensis. Exotic plants have been propagated in these gardens since the 1700s, and an awareness of Hibiscus existed as far back as the Medieval period, since it is mentioned by Dante in "Inferno." In Italy, Hibiscus is commonly planted for its ornamental value.
The Jerusalem Botanical Gardens, which has the most intensive compilation of plants not only in Israel, but in the entire Middle East, highlights a variety of hibiscus species, including Hibiscus schizopetalus, Hibiscus panduriformis, and Hibiscus coccineus.

Uses


Landscaping
Hibiscus species are grown for their showy flowers or used as landscape shrubs, and are used to attract butterflies, bees, and hummingbirds. In the Philippines, it is considered to be the Queen of the Garden. Hibiscus is used as an ornamental flower in tropical and sub-tropical zones worldwide. 


Rope and construction
The ropes on the missionary ship Messenger of Peace were made of fibres from hibiscus trees.


Food
Dried hibiscus is edible, and it is often a delicacy in Mexico. It can also be candied and used as a garnish, usually for desserts. Contrary to popular assumptions that the flowers or petals are what is being eaten, it is the calyces. Hibiscus sabdariffa, also known as "Jamaica" or roselle, is the species of hibiscus used to make herbal tea. Since it is sour, it is often mixed with honey, sugar, or cinnamon. In Tobago, it was used as fodder for animals.


Folk medicine
Hibiscus × rosa-sinensis is described as having a number of medical uses in Indian Ayurveda. In Tobago, it was used for hygienic purposes (dental.) Hibiscus has many health benefits, such as lowering blood pressure and providing antioxidants. In ancient Hawaii, chewing and swallowing the leaves was considered a natural laxative. Chewing its seeds was seen as a way of strengthening a feeble child. Extracts were used to prevent falling hair and dandruff, and other plant parts were considered valuable in fighting infections.


Precautions and contraindications


Pregnancy and lactation
While the mechanism is not well understood, previous animal studies have demonstrated anti-fertility effects of H. × rosa-sinensis. The H. × rosa-sinensis extract has exhibited contraceptive effects in the form of estrogen activity in rats. These findings have not been observed in humans. The H. × rosa-sinensis is also thought to have emmenagogue effects which can stimulate menstruation and, in some women, cause an abortion. Due to the documented adverse effects in animal studies and the reported pharmacological properties, the H. × rosa-sinensis are not recommended for use during pregnancy.


Symbolism and culture
The red hibiscus is the flower of the Hindu goddess Kali, and appears frequently in depictions of her in the art of Bengal, India, often with the goddess and the flower merging in form. The hibiscus is used as an offering to Kali and the god Ganesha in Hindu worship.
The pink hibiscus flower has its origins in Asia and the Pacific Islands, where it has served as a symbol of beauty, femininity, and young love. It is commonly associated with the Hawaiian culture and the Aloha spirit, which celebrates love, happiness, and peace. In Hawaii, it is used for decoration, particularly behind one's ear. In ancient times, they were used to create lei, which were short-lived but gorgeous.


As a national and state symbol
The hibiscus is a national symbol of Haiti, and the national flower of nations including the Solomon Islands and Niue.  Hibiscus syriacus is the national flower of South Korea, and Hibiscus × rosa-sinensis is the national flower of Malaysia. It is also the state flower of Hawaii.
grok_lead: Hibiscus is a genus of flowering plants in the mallow family, Malvaceae, comprising approximately 430 species that are native to warm-temperate, subtropical, and tropical regions worldwide. These plants exhibit diverse growth forms, ranging from annual and perennial herbs to shrubs, subshrubs, and small trees, and are characterized by their large, showy flowers with five equal petals that are typically funnel-shaped or flat, measuring from 2 inches to over 12 inches wide, and often lasting only one day. The flowers feature fused stamen filaments forming a sheath around the style, attracting pollinators such as hummingbirds and butterflies, while the bold foliage contributes to their ornamental appeal in gardens. The genus is the largest in the Malvaceae family, which also includes economically important plants like cotton and okra, and Hibiscus species are widely cultivated for horticultural purposes due to their striking blooms in shades of red, pink, white, yellow, and blue. Notable ornamental species include the tropical Chinese hibiscus ( Hibiscus rosa-sinensis), prized for its year-round flowering in warm climates, and hardy perennials like the swamp rose mallow ( Hibiscus moscheutos) and scarlet rose mallow ( Hibiscus coccineus), which thrive in moist soils and produce flowers up to 12 inches across. Additionally, Hibiscus syriacus (rose of Sharon) is a deciduous shrub valued for its cold hardiness in USDA zones 5-9 and adaptability to various soils, though it can become invasive in some areas. Beyond ornamentals, certain Hibiscus species hold significant economic and medicinal value; for instance, Hibiscus sabdariffa (roselle), an annual shrub native to West Africa, with cultivation extending to Asia and other tropical regions worldwide, is grown globally for its edible, crimson calyces, which are rich in anthocyanins, flavonoids, and organic acids. These calyces are primarily used in culinary applications such as teas, jams, sauces, and beverages for their tart flavor and natural red pigmentation, as well as in traditional medicine for their antihypertensive, antidiabetic, and antioxidant properties, with clinical trials demonstrating reductions in systolic blood pressure by up to 7.43 mmHg and improvements in lipid profiles after regular consumption. Additionally, extracts from various Hibiscus species are used in cosmetic products for their potential benefits to skin and hair health, including antioxidant effects that may support skin elasticity and hair nourishment, supported by preliminary scientific studies and traditional practices. Other species contribute to fiber production and cultural traditions, underscoring the genus's versatility across ecological and human contexts.
